voiceover: Parents want to add guests? Give them a number. Copy, Paste, Send. Today's awkward message: a parent adding to your guest list. I'm Norah, Wedillybird's AI host. Three messages, warm to firm. A veto starts a fight. A number starts a list. First, settle the number with your partner. Family who pitch in earn input. They don't earn the last word. Even if they pay for part, you can still cap their names. Message one, the warm opener. Thank them, give your number, ask for names. Thank you for helping! We have room for eight names from you. Could you send them by Friday? Ask both families for names early, before they trickle in. The step people skip: combine every name into one wish list first. Message two, for when both families are asking. We've set a cap for each side, so both families feel represented. Follow if you're planning ahead. Tomorrow: your wedding day, starting at the front door. Message three, the firm one. Point at the space or the budget, not the person. We're keeping the day small because of space. It's not personal; we'd love to celebrate with them afterwards. Then host something smaller, before or after the wedding. For everyone who missed the cut. Draw the line by relationship, not by person. One easy cutoff: first aunts, uncles and cousins. A very small wedding? Parents, siblings and grandparents only. Anyone who just misses goes on a ranked B-list. A B-list invitation is just a normal invitation. No apology needed. Thank them. Give the number. Keep the final say. The pinned comment has all three, word for word. Keep this for the first time a parent texts you a name. A number, not a veto.

caption:
Parents adding to your wedding guest list? Give them a number, not a veto. Three copy-and-paste messages from warm to firm, plus an easy way to draw the line by relationship.
Hosted by Norah, an AI character created by the Wedillybird team.
pinned_comment:
Copy, paste, send (swap in your own number and date):
1. The warm opener: "Thank you for helping! We have room for [number] names from you. Could you send them by [date]? We'll make the final list together."
2. A cap per side: "We've set a cap for each side, so both families feel represented."
3. The firm one: "We're keeping the day small because of space (or budget). It's not personal; we'd love to celebrate with them afterwards."
The formula: thank them, give the number, keep the final say.
Where to draw the line: by relationship, not by person. An easy cutoff is first aunts, uncles and cousins; for a very small wedding, parents, siblings and grandparents only (Zola). Anyone who just misses goes on a ranked B-list, and a B-list invitation is just a normal invitation, with no apology (Philadelphia Magazine, 2015).
Wording is suggested, not a quote. Positions from Zola (2025) and Philadelphia Magazine (2015).
Norah is AI-generated.

claims_review.notes: No statistics. 'Eight names' and 'Friday' in message one are fill-in examples (the pinned comment shows [number] and [date]). Message wording is suggested wording built on Zola's published positions (T26 'suggested wording'), not quotes; the overlay credits the positions, not the wording. Philadelphia Magazine is from 2015 (dated on screen); its B-list timing windows and the keep-groups-together rule, and the two-question friendship test, are deliberately not repeated here because other scripts in the series already teach them; this script uses T27's relationship-based cutoff instead.
